blocks.x: Steve Brown The Music World The Music World

Well, folks, my name is Steve Brown to the Music World. My real name is Ted Brown. I was born and raised in New Orleans, Louisiana. My parents had a musical background. I guess my brother and I, we were talented in that respect. We began playing early in our teens. And I guess just after our father and mother's death, we were quite young and we fooled around with different types of musical instruments and gradually decided to stay on one instrument. And the trombone was my brother's and bass fiddle was mine. And we played around New Orleans for years in all the best places in the city. And we had, up to 1913 when I left them, one of the best bands in the city. I left to follow my trade as sheet metal worker and proceeded to Jackson, Louisiana, the East Louisian State Hospital. After being there about three years, I married and came back to New Orleans for a little while and proceeded to Natchitoches, Louisiana, where I opened up a business of my own. I remained there for about three years and came back into the music field. That was in 1920. I arrived in Chicago. I arrived in Chicago. And to my surprise, no one was using bass fiddles. Everyone had tubers in the orchestras. And it seemed to be impossible for me to get a job. However, I continued to bother the best booker considered in Chicago at that time, Cope Harvey, and succeeded in getting a job date at the Blackstone Hotel. In order to get more work, I'd done everything I could to attract attention and succeeded in having the people gather around the band and refrain from dancing until we finished playing. I had no trouble from there after. Different contractors offered me jobs and in a short time I had all the work that I could do in Chicago. I remained there for, oh, up until 1926. And left to join the Goldcat Orchestra in Detroit. I signed a contract with Goldcat for five years. And remained with him doing that entire time. Until the band broke up in New York. And then I joined Whiteman. I may say that up until the time I reached Chicago, I never knew a note in music. I've never taken a lesson. And that when I was offered jobs in larger bands, it was necessary for me to learn how to read. So I had to put my mind to read. And I learned how to read good enough in which to cover different types of work in the orchestra field. And when I joined Whiteman, the music was a little different from me. It was a little symphonic in conjunction with rhythmically played pieces. And that seemed to worry me quite a bit. And I never enjoyed myself playing as much as much as I did with the Goldcat outfit. Because we played practically everything rhythmically. Only when we played shows would be considered differently. You know, ballads and things like that that we had to play. But, uh, I played. And it was satisfactory all right. I got by with the type of music that was put before me. And, uh, we were, Whiteman was offered a contract to terminate his recordings with the Victor people and go over to the Columbia. And they, in turn, were going to, uh, and they, in turn, were going to, uh, send the band around the world, visiting every principal city. And, uh, Paul had told me that he was willing to pay my wife's fare along with his orchestra, but that I'd have to leave the children on this side. And, uh, I consulted my wife about it. And she felt that if anything happened to the children while she was across water, she'd never forgive herself. And, uh, she urged me to go ahead and, and she'd remain on this side. Well, I wasn't feeling any too good at that particular time, so I decided to stay here, too, and, uh, told Paul about it. Well, the depression was setting in at that particular time, and the trip around the world was canceled for Paul. And Paul had to cut down his orchestra considerably. There was, uh, quite a number of boys left when I left. Tommy Darcy, Jimmy Darcy, uh, a little later Buzzy, and quite a lot of well-known boys left the orchestra. And then Paul, during the Depression days, had to sort two cheaper musicians, you know what I mean? And he got by the best way he could at that particular time. I returned to Detroit and played for Gene Goldkatt again. And then, uh, he sent me down to Chicago to start his new orchestra. He was starting a new orchestra called the WGN Orchestra, directed by Earl Stokes. Uh, Stokes. Uh, Stokes. An accordion player. And, uh, I didn't like the band, and, uh, so I told Gene Goldkatt to put someone else in my place, that I was going down to New Orleans and, uh, that I'd, uh, return back to Detroit later on. And if he had anything for me to do, I'd, I'd be glad to play for him again. So, that WGN band continued for a while and made some records. Uh, however, they didn't have any market for that type of orchestra, and it soon disbanded. I joined another unit of Goldkatt called the Vagabond, and traveled around the country a little bit with them, although we didn't make any records. I didn't make any records with the Vagabond. And, uh, I went down as far as San Antonio, Texas, and returned with them. And they made a trip later up east. And I failed to go with them. And, uh, I thought I'd remain locally and stay, uh, stay in Detroit. At that particular time, I wasn't feeling so good. And not knowing what was the matter with me, I soon found out that it was arthritis that I had. And, as the weeks and months grew, why I began to be crippled more and more until I had to confine myself indoors for a couple years or so. And, uh, after the, uh, attack of arthritis subsided a little bit, I tried to play music a little, but it didn't satisfy me. And I later on looked for other types of work to do, such as salesmanship. And later on, I took an examination of steam engineering. And, uh, I haven't, uh, played since, since then. And that was about, let's see, I've been out of the music field now for about 10 or 12 years. And, uh, up to that time, where I played with different organizations in Chicago. When I arrived in Chicago in 1920, I played with a lot of small Dixieland groups, uh, later larger orchestras, such as the Fryer's Inn band, and, uh, later with the Midway Garden Orchestra, which was when I started to learn how to read. And, uh, up to that time, of course, as I said before, I never knew a thing about music, and, uh, had no idea what it was all about until I went up and on it. But, uh, shut it off. I didn't know what to say.
Let's go. Let's start all over again, and I'll, I'll ask you a question. What date were you born and where?

I was born in January of 13, 1890, in New Orleans. And, uh, there was five of us born in New Orleans. Mm-hmm. We were all Christian and practically the same church, Father Lambert's church. That's a Catholic church. Yeah, Father, uh, Father.
What's, uh, Father Lambert saying? Father Lambert at that particular time. It's Our Lady of Good Counsel church now. Lady of Good Counsel. Yeah.

Yeah. Now, yeah. I see. However, my father was a Catholic, my mother was a Protestant, so later on my mother had brought us into the Protestant faith. However, my brother, Tom, had just passed away while he was buried in the Catholic faith. He was, his wife is Catholic, so she evidently had him to come, return back to the church. Mm-hmm. Uh, but anyway, in those particular days, we were in poor circumstances. So we were very young, when my mother passed away, my father passed away about, what was it, Louise? A year or two before my mother, huh? A year and ten months. A year and ten months before my, my mother passed away. And, uh, so we were quite small. I was twelve and Tom was fourteen. And in those days, why, we were in poor circumstances, and we had to work in the day and try to get a little education in the night by attending night school.
Selfie school? Selfie right school.
Well, yes. I attended selfie right school during the night, but none of us received any too much education.
Now, did your mother and father play music?

Yes. Uh, my father had a little band of his own. Well, not of his own, but he played in the band. I think he played different string instruments. Violin, different, uh, wands of them would get together, and they played different affairs. And my father was, uh, quite active in dramatics of different kinds. And his mother, my grandmother, on the brown side, was a piano teacher. And my, my grandmother on my mother's side also knew how to play piano. So, we were gifted in, in that respect. See, that's the reason we were able to pick up instruments and learn how to play them quickly.
Well, now, would your father be a faker, or did he read the music, or could he fake?
No, I think he played by ear. I think he played by ear.
Well, would he play what they call jazz now, Dixieland jazz?

Well, no. Not that particular time. There were lances, mazookas, and charlice, and reels, and there was no such thing as, uh, as ragtime music at that particular time. I see. Uh, it came, uh, ragtime came into effect a little after that, around the time when we were starting to play. Okay. Uh, that steel bread band was around there. I used to go around when I was a kid to hear him play. And we had what we called lawn parties, given practically every neighborhood around the city in those days. Particularly in the, uh, Negro sections that have tarpaulin spread over the yard in the back. The Negro bands would play, and as kids we'd go listen at them, you know, and we'd hear them play all types of tunes. But they didn't have what we call or considered the Dixieland combinations. See, and some of those bands went to New York and Chicago at different times and played, but their type of music wasn't considered a jazz type or Dixieland combination. They had violins and flutes and things like that in the hours, you see. And the real Dixieland combination consisted of five pieces, mainly. Sometimes they put six, sometimes they put seven or eight pieces.
Well, what instruments were those? Huh?

What instruments were those in the Dixieland? The main instruments, the main five instruments were cornet, trombone, cornet, drums, and we didn't have piano in those days. We had guitar. A great many guitar players played a twelve string guitar to give enough body and rhythm to be heard. In so many places they didn't have a piano for the musicians to play.
What were the horns? I didn't get the horns straight. I didn't get the horns straight.
Cornet, trombone, and clarinet, and then we used bass, guitar, and drum. And they added up to the musicians, right? Later on, after they got up north, well, they had to have piano.
The guitar wasn't loud enough or something.

Everybody had a habit of having a piano with all the bands, so the boys had to sit down here and get different piano players until they got the right one. I think reggae was with the Dixieland, wasn't it? Yeah.
Did they use any of these homemade instruments with those groups or did they use all regular instruments?

Well, at that particular time, they were, these boys had all batted up instruments, you know, maybe they bought, the majority of them bought them second handed. They couldn't afford to buy the new ones. They were too expensive for them. And later on, as they played, they played a lot of jobs while they got new instruments. But they were pretty high in those days. The instruments weren't so plentiful as they are today. And when we got an old batted instrument, we tried to repair it the best way we could and learn how to play something on it. Now we had what we call a fissured band around in New Orleans. One of the boys, by the name of Schilling, did you meet him? Happy? Yeah. Happy Schilling, yes. That's the one, yeah. Well, he's largely responsible for us playing. Tom and I, we decided to go batting at one time. And we read at the house and we furnished it. And the happy Schilling used to come over there and ask permission at different times to leave a lot of instruments over there. Trombone, tubas, clarinets, you know, different band instruments. Oh, we were tickling to death and let them leave it over there because Tom and I used to fool around with them during the day. And before we knew it, we knew how to play a lot of them, see. We just, out of curiosity, wanted to see if we could play them. We applied ourselves enough and sure enough we learned how to play. I played a little bit on the clarinet, the cornet, trombone, tubas, things like that. And Tom did the same thing. Well, Tom seemed to love trombone and I loved the bass more than I loved any other instrument. And we used to sit down at the piano, you know, and play, learn to play quite a few numbers on piano. And while we liked all the instruments, still the bass seemed to appeal to me. It seemed like I loved that instrument. And Tom seemed to love the trombone more than any other instrument too. So we, we stopped playing so well that we attracted attention and people started hiring us for different dances. No lessons on them.
No lessons on anything.

No lessons on anything. In fact, we had trumpet player Ray Lopez, he played the, his cornet, as I call it, because he was short, see. Left handed. Instead of right handed, he put his left hand over the horn and figured that way, left handed. Well, that was his style of playing. But he wasn't taught. The only one that knew how to read a few notes was Gussie Mueller. And he could only read the lead part on top of a piano part. And he'd play that over and we'd catch it just that quick, see, and we'd form our own harmony and rhythm to it. And that's the way we learned our numbers.
Now what was your first instrument that you took up?

Your very first one. Oh I strummed on guitar and flute and harmonica. I think I played harmonica first. Jews' harp and flutes. Things like that when I was a kid. And later on I got a hold of a guitar. I think my father's guitar was laying around the house. And we'd learn how to play and make all the changes. And they would call different boys in and teach them the changes. You know what I mean? And have them to play with us. So before long we had a little band and then we got a little larger band. And then we became known and we'd start playing at different affairs. How old were you then? Well as a time go along I guess I started at twelve so I must have been around fifteen or so. When we were really making headway and attracting attention. And so we were offered a job to play in the carnival parade for the Garden District Carnival Club. And they said if you can get a hold of a brass band and play as good as you do with your orchestra. Well we'll give you the job to the carnival. So we agreed to that. Well Tom and I were worried about getting uniforms to have for the men to play. So we joined the state militia. And we asked the captain to loan us the blue uniforms and the blue coats. And we got enough for the entire men. Ten men in this brass band. And everyone had to get white pants. See? And we had tan shoes and leggings. And freighting down the street we had the name of the band on top. See that covered the company's insignia. And we took off the cross guns. See? So we looked like we had band uniforms. Well the club at that particular year won first prize. And in the paper they mentioned how wonderful the band looked. You see? In the paper. So Tom didn't remember that. So I felt like going in the library and looking over the papers of that particular date. And see if I could get the clipping of that particular affair. So that was the first brass band affair that we played. And the club won first prize. And we had quite a nice mentioning about the band and how well we played.
How old were you for that parade then?
Oh I guess around 15 or 16 years.
Well we could find that in the paper in the library. We'll do that.
I was thinking about looking. I wanted Tom to go down with me. And I could look over the paper in that particular year.
We'll look it up. We'll find it. It might take a while but we'll do it.

Well yes. Well in a way. That was our first brass band job. Then we had became acquainted with Jack Lane. Jack Lane more or less had brass bands. He didn't fool around with orchestra much. He had a big brass band. He was a bass drummer himself. And whenever he had orchestra jobs, he'd give us a lot of orchestra jobs. But a great many times I'd play with Jack Lane and his band. He'd want me to play tuba for him. And Tom would be hired in different positions. We all worked along with different others. But we got so towards last that we were unable to play with anyone. We had enough jobs to keep us busy. In fact, some of the boys quit their work. We had Ray Lopez, a trumpet player. Why? He was playing enough to justify him in quitting work. He was making enough money just as it was. He wanted to sleep in the daytime. One question about Lopez. Was he really left-handed in everything he did?
Did he write left-handed and eat left-handed? Or just played the trumpet that way?

That I don't remember. You don't remember? I could ask him, but I don't remember whether he wrote left-handed or... Where is he now? In California? He's in California. He and Gussie Mueller are in California.
You know where they live and what part? Yes, I have their address.
Oh, we'd like to get that.
Because, you know, Nicola Rocca and Sharky both finger with the left hand.
Oh, by the way, Gussie Mueller's daughter's writing a story.
Oh, that's wonderful.

And she's writing a story, and I don't know whether it's supposed to be published pretty soon. And I think, from my understanding, they put me in the band. I said, well, I wasn't in the band when you first went up there. Well, Ray says you were in the band originally, so we put your name in the band. So we left Locanna out. So I said, no, that isn't fair. I said, Locanna was with the band when you first went up there. I had already quit. And when I came back in the field, of course, all this had been pioneered, but they hadn't had anyone to play bass like I did, see? Now, for instance, when we were playing in New Orleans, we played for all the prize fights. In those days, we played between each round to keep the fans satisfied. And then before the fights, we'd play and play and have the crowds applauding and put them in a good spirit, see? And to advertise a fight, we'd stand on different corners or go in a truck and play. So I was standing on Royal Street around Iberville or one of those streets down there in the business section. And many times when we were playing down there, a lot of men would poke their head over my shoulders and be watching me while I was playing. And some of them would say, my God, I've been traveling all around, but I never heard anybody play a bass like that. And to me, I thought they were just criticizing me, you know what I mean? I just figured that they were just thinking that I couldn't play. Well, it sounded good to me, so I didn't care. And up for a long time, I thought the same thing. Even when the people applauded me up north, I just figured they were just didn't mean it, you know? And even when the boys were raving about how well I played and they'd come pat me on the back and things like that, I still thought they were just chasing me, you see? And this Russ Morgan, he wrote an article some time back in the Post. He'd write practically everything about me and how when I first came there and how the people would come around to Bandstand. And Steve thought the people were just putting him on and things like that, you know? It was really a fact.
But tell her, where are those fights? Where did they have them?
Right here in New Orleans, New Orleans Athletic Club.
Not where?
Well, this one seemed to have been downtown. The stadium was, uh, seemed to have been on, uh...
The same place that it is now? Or did they carry it down?
No, they must have seen it now. The Coliseum.
The Coliseum, that's where...

Well, that's where... No, no, this one downtown. Just, uh, about two or three blocks below Canal Street. In the middle of a block of one place. I think it was between Royal and the, uh, Royal and something on the, on the downtown side. Charter, sure, I know that. Some old place they had, Athletic Club, or rather the pavilion was there.

Yeah, that's where the, uh, courthouse is now, I think, for a while. Maybe so. Yeah, have a picture of that. It would either be Royal and Charters or Royal and Bourbon, wasn't it? About St. Louis, uh, street walking there. Oh, which of Royal County was it? I could find out the correct address. I know, I could check on that now. I know what you mean, I think.

Well, anyway, uh, the people that stand around and listen at the band, particularly these strangers, the out-of-town people, they'd come around and, oh, they'd just holler, you know, maybe we'd hear that type of music. So, I guess it was that, uh, kind of music Tom was playing at the Yacht Club or someplace where Fishburne was dancing. And, uh, the thing that I knew was that, uh, caused Frisco to go back up to New York to tell, uh, tell the people in Lamb's Cafe about the band he heard down in New Orleans. But, anyway, we played all the Yacht Clubs and the Germanistic Clubs, and we played for, uh, all the best people in New Orleans at that particular time up to the time I left them. And we were rated very highly by all the public in general as being a very good band, one of the best bands down in New Orleans. But, uh, they never, uh, the newspapers never did give it to write up like they do today. They mentioned a lot about the musicians and bands. But in those days they just said the band had, maybe they may say had a good orchestra, you know, a name or something like that. But generally the band's name and that's about all of them was.
Well, which Lai Canna was it that you mentioned, uh? Arnold Lai Canna. Arnold, huh? He went up to, with Tom.

Oh, I see. He took my place when I left, when I left the band in 1913. He took my place and played from then on. Uh, played in Chicago and went to New York with them. And, uh, the going got pretty rough in New York, I understand, for Tom and them. And, uh, Lai Canna and Lambert and Shields, I think, beat it out of New York. One other question. What did you call that band down here? What was the name of it? Well, we, uh, we called it just Brown's Band. Brown's Band. And sometimes some people would put across on the streamer at picnics that we played, Brown's Ragtime Band, see? And that's all. But it was just known as Brown's Band. Who was really the leader? Well, we called Ray Lopez the leader. Tom was the manager. I was nobody for that matter, but I'd go around and book the band. I was a booker and I'd keep the boys working, because in the daytime I'd watch all the papers, every affair that was being given. You know, I'd go see the chairman of the committee and sell him on the idea of the band, see? And tell him who we played for. And after I told him who we played for and had them to verify my statement why, I'd get the job very easy, because we did have a good band. And I'm acquainted with all the musicians that are well known down in New Orleans at that particular time.
What pieces did you play then? Do you remember some of the numbers?

We played the same pieces that are played today, only they all have different names. See, we used to call them meatballs and snot, number two. We'd make up a lot of these numbers and we'd just give them a name that way, see? Just joking. And a great many times, one of the fellas would start off and I would ask what he was going to play and he said, well, that's alright, just follow me. So if it sounded good, he'd try to repeat the same thing, you know, then we'd play it different each time, but gradually it would simmer down into one type of number. So in those days, the rock used to come up before he could play trumpet and he used to sit up alongside of Ray Lopez on Ringo Magazine, we used to play up there. And he used to learn how to play the same notes that Raymond Lopez played. And he soon learned how to play the numbers. And Eddie Edwards used to play fiddle at first, see? And his father bought him a trombone and he told me, he says, take Eddie around with you. And he says, let Eddie sit in and learn how to play his trombone. So I took Eddie around with me and pretty soon Eddie started picking up on his trombone, see? And so that's how Eddie Edwards started on his trombone. But they couldn't play before, we were playing long before on the locker and Edwards was playing. Sheegans was just, well, he was a pretty good clarinet player but he was nothing in comparison to Gus Emuha, see? And he couldn't play as many numbers as Gus Emuha. You can shut that off.

Well, it was just about, this tape is just about over now. Yeah, it's just about over. Yeah. I was going to ask, what was number two? What was that tune, I remember? Number two was Tiger Rack. What was the Tiger Rack? And what's the name now of Meatball? I think that was Dixley and Winstead. I don't know what the boys up there gave it.
Oh, yeah. Names again. I think it was Dixley and Winstead. Okay, this is the end of this game here. Oh, yeah. Oh, yeah. Oh, yeah. Oh, yeah. I think it was Dixley and Winstead.
Okay, this is the end of this game here. Oh, yeah. Oh, yeah.

You were talking about Eddie Edwards, he was smart in organizing, right? Well, he knew the trouble of Tom Ed in Chicago, see? Tom was up there, the band was going so good and attracting so much attention that the band leaders would try to break up Tom's band by trying to offer one man a little bit more money, see? And some of them would quit Tom, and Tom would come back to the laws and get someone else, that's the way it was. So, in order to avoid that trouble, Eddie Edwards incorporated the band, see?
George Brunis and his family.
Tom got his way out to home.
Tom got a nice ride up there.

He deserved credit. Well, he was, in reality, a pioneer in the jazz field. And there was other colored bands that were up there. This was before Louis Armstrong came up there. This was before King Oliver and all those came up. King Oliver and the bands that King Oliver played, and Armstrong, when they first come up to New Orleans, it wasn't a Dick's land combination at all. They had violins, they had flutes, and they had about eight, ten, twelve men, so you understand. And they played regular music at all the other colored pieces. But the Dick's land combination, just five pieces, that's entirely different.
Yeah, Oliver, I think, got there about 1918, she saw it. And you say Papa Lane had mostly just the brass band. Mostly the brass band. And didn't do much dance work. No.

He'd take it to the small band. But I mean, you could see what... He'd play drums if he, maybe in the small combination. But I mean, I don't remember seeing, we didn't have no competition with these bands at all. In fact, the only bands that gave us competition, in respect, was Fisher's Band. And that band there, in the estimation of the dancers, and the people that I talked to that employed us, were second-raders in comparison to our band. And we played all the most exclusive affairs in New Orleans, up to the time I left them, in 1950.
You say Papa Lane would turn some of his dance jobs over to you then, when he'd got them?
Oh, yes. A great many times he'd have bands, he'd dance us downtown, and he'd give us a job. Did you ever work? And of course, he'd get his booking fees. Yeah.
Did you ever work in any band with Jack Lane? Jack Lane? Jack Lane?
Yes, I played tuba with Jack Lane, Jack Lane quite a number of times, across the river, as I remember, different affairs.
Would that be dancers or...? Dances, yeah, dancers. What sort of a rhythm did he get?

See, we used to employ brass bands for dances too, great big dances. Now, they used to have dances out in all the bands, all the large pavilions that have a very big brass band in order to be heard. Well, that was the habit. But later on, like in Mellenburg and in West End, they had certain pavilions out there, but it all depended upon the chairman of the committee. If he wanted an orchestra, he'd specify an orchestra, you know. Or if he wanted to hire a brass band, he'd hire a brass band. But as a general rule, the orchestra used to sound better to the dancers in the brass band. In fact, they could dance much better than they could to the brass band. The brass band couldn't get into the groove like the orchestra would come.
Do you remember who was in the Papa Lane's band? Any of the other musicians that you can think of now? Papa Lane's band?
I remember a lot of them, but the names I can't. You'd have to get that for Jack Lane himself. I imagine he remembers all the names of them.
One clarinetist, Bach K, did you ever know him?

Bach K, yes. I remember him. I think he played with the band quite a bit. He played for Jack Lane. Bach K used to have time, play job dates with us. Maybe when Gussie Mule was sick or couldn't get off or something happened. Bach K and Yellow Nunez and Shields and different ones at different times. The same as Harry Shields, who play with different combinations around here now. And you'd see him on television with, what's this little short caller's name again? Shockey. Shockey. And he'd play around with different combinations, any place that'll offer him money, you know. And that's the same way with the musicians' world when I was down here up until 1915.
Do you remember a fellow named Dave Perkins? I think he played trombone. Dave Perkins, yes.

He was an outstanding fellow at that particular time. He played. I didn't like his playing as well as I did Bad Frank. That's when I was little. I remember Dave Perkins when I was little. And they had a bass player, a colored bass player. I can't think of his name now. He was a light complected Creole sort of a fellow. He played a good bass. I used to admire him with the colored bands. He used to play a good bass and played the good notes, as I call them, you know.
Do you remember which band he played with?
I think he played with the Creole band. A band called himself the Creole band. I think the Creole band used to be around our neighborhood.
It couldn't be Bill Johnson.

I think they lived on, I think one of the members lived on 6th near Law Street, on the downtown side. And they used to hold rehearsals. They were rehearsals quite often. They had violins and things like that, and flutes in the band. And we lived around the corner from them, and I used to hear them rehearse. I think he was a bass player.
Oh, Gaspar, did you ever know him?
That name's familiar to me, but I just can't. He's a colored bass player.
I mean, he's pretty long. Yeah, I never did know him. He was a bass player.

Well, they used to have a professor, they used to teach music. I think his name was Barnett. He was a bass player. And the whole family played music. And we were at one time, we went over to that place to play for the old man. And I remember the old man being a teacher in legitimate music. It was just amazing to him to see how he played so well without using notes, you know what I mean? And everything from memory and completely dependent upon the air. To him, that was quite a sensation. And Brookhoven, I remember three-year-old Brookhoven. I did. I went over to each place one time, and I took one lesson. Or two. Two. After he gave me one lesson, I figured I knew I'd know. I had the idea. He just showed me how to blow it, you know. And old man Brookhoven. Theodore Brookhoven was the one that gave me my first carnival job for the parades. Now I'm not talking about the first carnival job we played for the Garden District Club, but for the floats in between the, you know, the bands in between the floats. We had professional bands. No school bands as they are now. Like the Rex Parade?
There was a big one?

Of course, I'm sorry I'll have to differ with Tom in that respect. Wasn't meant at all. It was taken, as I believe, from a French word. A jazzer. A jazzer to pep up. To accelerate. See? That's a French word. And it evidently could have been some French person that used that particular expression. And didn't give it the name of jazz. J-S-S at first. Then later on it was spelled J-A-C. Louis Armstrong was born July the 4th. I just wrote this down a lot of times. Yeah, yeah. And he joined King Oliver's band at Lincoln Garden Cafe in July 1922 in Chicago. So, that's the time he came up there.
Much later. See?

That's much later. Joseph King Oliver was born in 1885 on Dryde Street in New Orleans. I guess you saw that in the books. Yeah. Well, I copied a lot of things that I read out of the books in here. The notation. I thought maybe I'd read some of these. Did you ever read Charles Delaney's book?
Mm-hmm.
Columbia's $64 Jazz album. Oh, some of the... $64 Jazz album. Oh, yeah.
Yes, I've seen some of that.
And then, uh... Oh, I guess that was from the show. $64,000. Yes, that's an LP.
All right. Uh...
Maxine Skelton. Did you read his article?
No, I don't read that.
He mentions Tom Brown on page five. Puts Kelly with Dixieland band.
Kelly?

Yeah. And the rocker has... Well, there's a lot of them got everything mixed up in the writings, you know. Yeah. Well, it's good for you to correct it. Well, that's what I had in mind when I wrote to the university. So, if there was any questions that they wanted to ask me regarding different ones like that, according to what the books state or what they're trying to accept, I could tell them as much as I know about it, because I should remember what was going on. Now, there's Jazz Waves, volume number one by Rosenzal. Did you read that? Yes. You have that? And Frontiers of Jazz. Yeah.
Do you have any corrections you want to make on those?
Well, there are a lot of things. I'd have to look over the book again and order that. Oh, yeah.
Well, anytime you want to write us about that, we'd appreciate it.

Well, I intend to, when I write this book, I intend to bring in, mention different books and state what I know to be wrong. You know what I mean? To get my version of it anyway, and to hell with whoever wants to believe it, you know. I mean, I'm going to get my version of it, because after all these fellows wrote, they get their version of it. So why not me? Sure. I was born where hell before they were, so I should know a little more in that respect. The only thing I'm, and I got all the, I hear you talking to you, I hear you talking to you, the story of Jazz Buddy. Now, who put all those stories in there? Did you?
No, no, no. Some fellow in New York.
Well, he seemed to have gone all over and interviewed different positions.
A lot of that he got out of Downbeat. A lot of those interviews came out of Downbeat, published years ago. They did? And others were made in New York.
He interviewed someone in New York.

Well, I noticed he interviewed different musicians who talked. Well, he's never interviewed me, and I don't guess he stopped in Detroit. No, no. But he, La Cana, he talked to La Cana, and Johnny Stein. Now, Johnny Stein was another drummer, he was a drummer in New Orleans. Yeah. He was looked up to as quite a good drummer in those olden days. And, uh, there was another drummer by the name of Stevenson. Not Ragbabel Stevenson, but another Stevenson. I can't think of his first name as quite a fine drummer, too. Uh, they all played ragtime. Now, here, this fellow, Rudy, bless, had quite a lot of good ideas. He said, they all played ragtime, which is true. It was all ragtime before it was, uh, called jazz. So, it's still the same type of music, going to call jazz. Now they're changing it around to progressive jazz and swing and what have you, you know? Yeah. Uh, oh yeah. There's one fellow claimed that when he visited New Orleans, he went down on Bianville Street and met someone playing piano, you know? And there's quite a story in there. And, uh, he talks about a lot of colored musicians, too. I wrote all these down, so later on, when I get ahold of these books again, I can, uh, look over each one of them separately and then comment on different ones, you know? Uh, mention the names, see, of the book. Now, the history of jazz in America, did you read that? No, I don't. You didn't read that?
Is that Ullunoff? Who is that? Ullunoff?
Oh, no, I don't know. Yeah, Barry Ullunoff.
Mm-hmm.
Oh, yeah, I saw that. He's not so much. He... He gives you his viewpoints, but he's all screwed up. Did you ever read it? Yeah, I read it. Huh? I read it.
He's written two or three books, too. Yeah.

Oh, yeah, he's got several books, I think. Yeah. But boy, he's all wet on a lot of things. I forget not just what it was. Mm-hmm. New York was, uh, let's see, what was it? New York was a sad fourth, tenth, or twentieth, and... Oh, yeah. He tells about New York, which was true. New York was very slow on accepting jazz. Not like Chicago. New York was very slow. So that's the reason Tom had such a terrible time when he went to New York.
I wanted to ask you about some of those bands he played with in New York. Did he play with Yerks? Yerks?

Yerks band, yeah. Yerks. He played with Yerks. Hear me talking to you, Reinhardt & Company, Incorporated, New York. You know, you read that? Yes. And, uh, I don't know, I kinda has a full story on page 81. I got down there most of all lives. Another one by Johnny Stein. Read Johnny Stein's, page 32, 83, 84. Now, that's you hear me talking to you, yeah. I got little notations. I got shining trumpets.
Did you read that?

Yeah. And, uh, there's a lot of them are really nice. And they're nicely written up, and, uh, they just go out of a dream, or, uh, some fellow writes a book out in these states down in the 10-line district from the beginning to the end. You know what? And an ordinary person reading the book, they're going to say, my Jesus Christ, the brown band must have come right to my whole house. And we never did play around there. And our music wouldn't have been, as I told you before, it wouldn't have been acceptable for any type of music. You know the type of music they played down there in comparison to the type of music we played up here, so you couldn't consider that. Yet these writers would have the people believe it. If they knew. Well, I shouldn't.
We all hung around Tom and Hanksons enough.
My God, I used to go down there. I guess that's before your days, isn't it? Yeah, yeah. Let's see. What time did they break up that dreadlight district?
We broke that up around, I don't know, 32, 35.

We used to have the house of all nations, you see. You go in there and you paid so much. And you were fed, you take your time, you know. It may take days, but you go all around. Go down every national in the world, you go around. Great big hallway there, rooms, rooms, you know, all around. And here's Japan, China, oh, you got to go through it. That is, if you want to go through it. You can drop out if you want, but you pay your money and you're recording this.
That's alright. Somebody, it doesn't make any good. It doesn't make any good. That doesn't music. No.
But anyway, in those particular days, they had the type of music entirely different from what we played. And it couldn't be classed as that type of music.
No, I see what you mean.

And I'm only sorry that they didn't have any recordings. We didn't have any recordings in those days. Nothing to record by. Otherwise, you'd see what I mean. There are some musicians that can, some old piano players, some of these old colored piano players that you contact, they'll play the barrel house music for you. And they'll play all that type of music that you should play down there. And you'll be surprised. It can't be classified as the same as the type we played.
Are there any other records that you've made that you wanted to mention as outstanding for people to hear?
Well, they don't do me any good. I got paid for the, I got paid for the side.
I just thought you might want people to hear.

I do know that there's a lot of record collectors that are after the records. They've wrote me and asked me if I'd ever know when they're going to release some more of them. And I'd like to get some, I've had different musicians from Australia, some from England and France. They wanted to get other copies of it. Asked me if there's any releases coming. I don't know anything about it. In fact, it doesn't mean anything to me. There's no money in my pocket. And I told them I don't know just when they're releasing. But they do. Every now and then they'll come out with a group of numbers of different bands, you know, like they did with this cold catch. Now they sold out all these. In fact, I can't buy any. I've been looking for some. And I certainly appreciate you giving me. By the way, where is it? Here it is. There it is right there.
One question here about some of Tom's pieces. Do you remember some of his titles, the pieces that he wrote?

Yes, he had some numbers that he published. And I don't know, he didn't have them in the hands of the right people. They weren't plugged much. The only one that plugged it was him himself. I didn't, I myself, I didn't think much of them. I didn't think that they had any good commercial value to them. So, but let him have his fun, you know. There's a lot of people that write numbers, you know what I mean? That's mean anything. But he did have some numbers, wrote some numbers and had them published.
Do you remember the number June?
June, yeah.
That's when it came.

Yeah. And he had something to do with, what's the Spanish number? Rose of Spain. Rose of Spain. We have a piano roll of that, Love Dreams. He had some, did he have, did he put that on Rolls, Love Dreams? Yeah.
And the Halfway House recorded Love Dreams too, I believe.
Do you remember a piece, Our Bungalow of Dreams?
Bungalow of Dreams, yes I remember that.
Is that his, do you think? It was by a brown, but it has an E on the end of it.

Yeah, well, it seemed like I heard Tom speak of that, but now whether that's his or not I couldn't say. I've never seen the music to it or anything, but I've heard Tom speak of it. That's right. There's another brown with E on it, that means he's Irish. And we're English, so the B-R-O-W-N's. Yeah. And if he puts E on it, it's Irish. But I heard Tom speak about that, now whether he wrote it, I don't think he did.
Where do you think hot music originated? Hot music? Or ragtime, or whatever you want.
All down in this particular section of country.
And what does that include? Does that include any particular states or only one, or what?

More so down in New Orleans. It was all through the plantations and things like that. The old Negroes out there, I used to many times when I was a kid go along the river, and these Negro roasterabouts would be sitting out on a cotton bale waiting for the boats. And they'd be singing. And they'd harmonize so beautifully, you know what I mean? Oh, you never heard anything like it in your life. I'd just sit around there and listen to them for hours. And they'd just sing until the boat was ready to be loaded. And they'd have to go to work then. But I'd sit around, and some of them would bring the instrument, some of them would have a banjo or something. Some of them would have a trumpet, an old batted up trumpet. And they'd play their tune, some popular number, like they think it should be played, you know, improvising and playing it in their way, their style. And like I heard a Negro one time in one of the churches playing an organ. And instead of playing the organ like you would ordinarily play, he'd make a lot of arpeggio notes, you know, on the basses. And he had a rhythm going of his own. It sounds just like an orchestra in those days, see? And that's his way of playing. But I think hot music originally started right down here in New Orleans. And it all drifted in here from the plantations, you know. You could find it like in Baton Rouge, all that center, you'd find music coming through there. And in New Orleans the same way. We'd all get ideas from all around that section. And then for harmony, we used to love to pass by these Negro churches and hear them sing. And in the harmony, we used to love to hear how... ... ... ...

segments.title: Opening and Brown's own career summary
segments.summary: Brown gives an unprompted sketch of his life: New Orleans, Chicago from 1920, Goldkette, Whiteman, arthritis; the interviewer asks to restart.

segments.title: Birth, church and orphaned childhood in New Orleans
segments.summary: Born 1890; family church; parents died when he was twelve and Tom fourteen; night school.

segments.title: Musical parents and ragtime before Dixieland
segments.summary: Father played string instruments by ear, grandmothers taught piano; lawn parties and Black bands in New Orleans with violins and flutes, before ragtime.

segments.title: Instrumentation of the real Dixieland combination
segments.summary: The five or six-piece combination of cornet, trombone, clarinet, bass, guitar and drums; piano came later up north.

segments.title: Learning instruments without lessons; Happy Schilling and Gussie Mueller
segments.summary: Secondhand instruments, Schilling leaving instruments at the house, Tom and Ted teaching themselves bass and trombone; Ray Lopez and Mueller.

segments.title: First brass band job for a carnival club
segments.summary: Borrowed militia uniforms for a ten-piece brass band in the Garden District carnival parade; they plan to find the clipping.

segments.chapter: Brown's Band and Tom in Chicago
segments.title: Jack Lane, Ray Lopez and Brown's bass playing
segments.summary: Jack Lane's brass band passed on jobs; Lopez left-handed; Brown's bass drew comments from strangers; confusion over who was in the band in Chicago.

segments.title: Playing prize fights and society clubs in New Orleans
segments.summary: Playing at the athletic club fights and yacht clubs; discussion of the fight venue's location; the band's high standing.

segments.title: Brown's Band: leadership, booking and repertoire
segments.summary: Lopez leader, Tom manager, Ted booker; LaCarna took his place in 1913; tunes with joke names; Eddie Edwards learns trombone.

segments.chapter: Brown's Band and Tom in Chicago
segments.title: Eddie Edwards incorporates Tom's Chicago band
segments.summary: Edwards incorporated the band so rivals could not poach its men.

segments.chapter: Brown's Band and Tom in Chicago
segments.title: Dixieland combination versus older Black orchestras; competition
segments.summary: Brown's band was a pioneer; Oliver and Armstrong's earlier bands were larger with violins; only Fisher's band competed.

segments.title: Working with Jack Lane and brass bands versus orchestras for dances
segments.summary: Lane passed on dance jobs, Brown played tuba with him, and orchestras suited dancers better than brass bands.

segments.title: Bakay and other musicians who subbed in the band
segments.summary: Bakay, Yellow Nunez and Shields substituted at times; musicians moved between combinations.

segments.title: Early Black bass players and the Creole band
segments.summary: Dave Perkins, an unnamed Creole bass player with the Creole band, and Gaspar are discussed.

segments.title: Professor Barnett, Theodore Brockhoven and the first Mardi Gras parade job
segments.summary: A short lesson from a teaching family, then Brockhoven books Brown's band for the carnival parades with bands between floats.

segments.title: Arthritis, leaving Whiteman and the diet that eased it
segments.summary: Whiteman had him play solos; pain in his fingers was diagnosed as arthritis; he changed diet and regained some use but quit playing.

segments.chapter: Brown's Band and Tom in Chicago
segments.title: Tom's band in Chicago and New York, via Ray Lopez's letters
segments.summary: Brown relays Lopez's reports: Lamb's Cafe packed in Chicago, a cool reception in New York, members scattering.

segments.chapter: Brown's Band and Tom in Chicago
segments.title: Identifying Bakay and a bassist named Bro
segments.summary: Brown cannot name Bakay's first name and suggests Chink; the interviewer asks about a bassist who knew him from Ellington's band.

segments.title: Playing opposite Ellington and Armstrong at Roseland
segments.summary: Two bandstands at Roseland, with Armstrong clowning, and daytime recording with night dances.

segments.title: McKinney's Cotton Pickers, Horvath and the WGN band
segments.summary: Charlie Horvath promoted the Cotton Pickers and organized Goldkette's WGN band, which sold poorly next to the Victor records.

segments.title: Playing Goldkette records: stock arrangements and slap bass
segments.summary: Brown explains how the band adapted stock orchestrations, notes the last record, Venuti, Don Murray's clarinet parts, and his slap bass.

segments.title: Grofe's bass number and identifying the WGN band record
segments.summary: Grofe wrote a slap-bass piece for Brown; a record turns out to be the WGN band, and Brown criticizes the bassist's tone.

segments.title: Clementine, My Pretty Girl and a homemade copy of the records
segments.summary: The group plays records, sorts out which are Brown's, and compares a homemade Detroit recording.

segments.title: Tracing records to the Goldkette and WGN bands
segments.summary: Brown cannot place several records, joined Goldkette in 1926, and guesses the McKinney group may have been mixed in.

segments.title: Vocal sisters on Goldkette recordings
segments.summary: Keller, Boswell and other sister acts; a Don Murray clarinet break.

segments.title: Eddie Lang, bowing the bass and Joe Venuti
segments.summary: On a record with Eddie Lang Brown says he used the bow on non-hot pieces; Venuti remembered as a clown.

segments.chapter: Origins of jazz and the district
segments.title: Red-light district music was not early jazz
segments.summary: Brown rejects the writers' view that jazz came from the district; its barrelhouse, slow-drag music differed from his lively dance music.

segments.chapter: Origins of jazz and the district
segments.title: Barrelhouse music and slow drags explained
segments.summary: Barrelhouse is slow bluesy piano with small groups; chatter about a visitor arriving.

segments.chapter: Origins of jazz and the district
segments.title: Never played in the district; Fisher and Blessing bands
segments.summary: His band never played the district, the name jazz arrived in Chicago, Fisher's band was good, and Tom's success drew copycat bands.

segments.chapter: Brown's Band and Tom in Chicago
segments.title: Tom with Ray Miller and Burt Kelly's Stables
segments.summary: Tom played with Ray Miller's Memphis Melody Boys in a Chicago show and at Kelly's Stables, where Brown sat in briefly.

segments.chapter: Origins of jazz and the district
segments.title: Jelly Roll Morton, the word jazz and Armstrong and Oliver dates
segments.summary: Brown remembers hearing Morton in Chicago, offers a French derivation for the word jazz, and cites dates for Armstrong and Oliver.

segments.title: Jazz books and Brown's plan to correct them
segments.summary: He reviews books by Delaunay, Shapiro, Rosenthal and others, and plans his own book correcting them.

segments.title: Rudi Blesh, Johnny Stein and New York's slow acceptance of jazz
segments.summary: Comments on books and interviews, ragtime as the earlier name, and New York's slowness to accept jazz.

segments.title: Writers' mistakes about Tom's band and the district
segments.summary: Tom played with Yerkes in New York; writers place the Brown band in the district; the House of All Nations; no recordings of that era.

segments.title: Collectors and records Brown made
segments.summary: Brown gets no money from the records but collectors abroad want them.

segments.title: Tom's published compositions
segments.summary: Tom's songs such as June, Rose of Spain and Love Dreams; uncertainty about Bungalow of Dreams.

segments.title: Where hot music originated
segments.summary: Brown says hot music began in New Orleans from plantation singing, riverfront roustabouts and church music.
